definition: Temerity means reckless boldness that defies rank, rules, or warnings; audacity.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word temerity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know temerity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Fresh from her first sale, the junior agent had the temerity to ask the firm's founding partner for his corner office when he retired - three decades early, as he saw it.
Boldness takes the initiative and may be admirable; temerity has already left admiration behind.
Daring runs real risks with open eyes; temerity goes further - risk-taking so heedless of consequence and rank that onlookers wince.

Nerve is informal boldness — the cheek to try it, said over the back fence and often half in admiration. Temerity is its formal, frowning cousin: boldness so heedless of rank, rules, or warnings that the speaker plainly disapproves.

Gall is brazen presumption that offends — demanding what decency forbids, with no visible shame. Temerity is wider and less self-serving: it covers overstepping toward danger as well as toward rank, and it stresses the heedlessness of the boldness rather than its shamelessness.

Recklessness is pure disregard of danger, and it needs no boldness at all — you can be reckless out of sheer inattention, texting through a red light. Temerity needs the bold gesture: an overstep against rank, rules, or warnings, made without ever weighing the cost.
careful weighing of risk
shrinking from any risk at all

Latin temere, 'blindly, rashly,' left almost nothing else in English - temerarious exists, but you may never meet it outside old court opinions. Beware the sound-alike timidity, from a different root entirely (timere, 'to fear'): temerity charges in blindly, while timidity will not charge at all.
Temerity means reckless boldness that defies rank, rules, or warnings; audacity.
The new deckhand untied the harbor master's own skiff to run a forgotten lunch out to the fleet, returning it with an emptied fuel tank and a cheerful wave.
The harbor master, speechless, finally produced the only word that fit: temerity - boldness so heedless of rank and consequence it looped past bravery into recklessness.
Temerity is not courage, though it borrows courage's costume: courage weighs the risk and accepts it; temerity never does the weighing.
The word always carries a raised eyebrow - the speaker thinks the boldness was rash, presumptuous, or both.
Temerity always disapproves a little: use it when boldness overstepped - toward danger or toward rank.
You met audacious in Unit 3; audacity can still be admiring, but temerity rarely is.
Informally, nerve and gall live in the same neighborhood; caution and timidity are its opposites.

The letter reached the maestro's office in June: eleven neat bars of his celebrated recording, copied out, with a second-year conservatory student's note that the horns were a half-step wrong.
His assistant filed it under a word the office reserved for such mail: temerity.
Students did not correct the maestro; warnings to that effect were practically printed on the conservatory's walls.
The student had asked no one and weighed nothing.
She mailed it the hour she noticed, rank be hanged.
In August a remastering engineer, working from the original tapes, flagged the same eleven bars.
The maestro never replied.
But the corrected pressing shipped that winter, and somewhere in the liner notes, unsigned, is the sentence 'with thanks to a sharp-eared friend.'
